question: How far does language modeling get when LSTMs are scaled to billions of parameters using modern LLM techniques while fixing known LSTM limitations?
hypothesis: LSTMs extended with exponential gating and matrix memory can match or beat Transformers and state space models at scale.
contributions: Exponential gating with normalization and stabilization
sLSTM: scalar memory, scalar update, new memory mixing (heads)
mLSTM: matrix memory, covariance update rule, fully parallelizable
xLSTM blocks (pre/post up-projection) residually stacked into xLSTM architectures
Language-model experiments up to 1.3B parameters and 300B tokens against Transformers, SSMs, RNNs

method.summary: Adds exponential gating (sLSTM) and a matrix memory with covariance update (mLSTM) to the LSTM, wraps them in pre-LayerNorm residual blocks, and trains decoder-style language models. Compared on 15B tokens (13 baselines) and then 300B tokens (RWKV-4, Llama, Mamba) of SlimPajama at 125M to 1.3B, plus synthetic tasks, MQAR and Long Range Arena.

evidence.where: Table 3 caption; text and tables use 350M

results.claim: At 15B SlimPajama tokens and ~350M-class size, xLSTM[1:0] has the lowest validation perplexity of 14 methods.
results.setup: All models match a GPT-3 350M (emb dim 1024, 24 residual blocks), 15B tokens SlimPajama, ctx 2048, bs 256, peak LR 1e-3, one epoch (step 28170); one run each (no seeds stated)
results.table: Table 1, row xLSTM[1:0], column SlimPajama (15B) ppl

results.claim: xLSTM[7:1] is second best in the same comparison.
results.table: Table 1, row xLSTM[7:1], column SlimPajama (15B) ppl

results.claim: Ablation morphing a vanilla LSTM into xLSTM: vanilla multi-layer LSTM is untrainable-bad (ppl 2417.86); resnet backbone, up-projection, exponential gating, matrix memory each cut perplexity, ending at 13.48.
results.setup: 15B SlimPajama tokens; 24-layer 1536-hidden PyTorch LSTM start; params 607.8M -> 408.4M

results.claim: Adding exponential gating takes ppl from 26.01 to 17.70 and adding matrix memory from 17.70 to 13.48.
results.quote: The ablation studies attribute the strong performance improvement to both the exponential gating and the matrix memory.

results.claim: Gating ablation: input-dependent and learnable forget and input gates give 13.43 versus 13.95 for fixed (non-learnable) forget bias [3,6] with no input gate dependence.
results.setup: xLSTM[1:0] with sigmoid forget gate and exponential input gate, 15B tokens
results.table: Table 2 (bottom), row Forget Gate + Input Gate

results.claim: Pre up-projection block with causal convolution is the best mLSTM block variant; without convolution ppl is 15.41.
results.table: Table 8, row Pre Up-Projection Block, With Convolution

results.claim: At 300B tokens, 1.3B xLSTM[1:0] has the lowest SlimPajama validation perplexity of the four models; xLSTM[7:1] is 9.00.
results.setup: 1.3B models (1422.6M actual params), 300B SlimPajama tokens, ctx 2048, bs 512, 300k steps
results.table: Table 3, 1.3B block, row xLSTM[1:0], column SlimPajama (300B) ppl

results.claim: Average accuracy over six common-sense tasks at 1.3B: xLSTM[1:0] 58.48, Mamba 58.41, xLSTM[7:1] 58.10; the margin to Mamba is 0.07 points.
results.setup: 1.3B, 300B tokens; LAMBADA, HellaSwag, PIQA, ARC-E, ARC-C, WinoGrande via LM Evaluation Harness; single run
results.note: Margin is within what one seed could change; no seeds or intervals reported. Mamba is best on ARC in some sizes (text concedes).
results.table: Table 3, 1.3B block, row xLSTM[1:0], column Average acc

results.claim: At 125M, average downstream accuracy xLSTM[7:1] 44.16 vs Mamba 43.63, Llama 41.78, RWKV-4 41.12.
results.table: Table 3, 125M block, row xLSTM[7:1], column Average acc

results.claim: At 760M xLSTM[1:0] average accuracy 56.12 versus Mamba 53.86 and Llama 52.74.
results.table: Table 3, 760M block, row xLSTM[1:0], column Average acc

results.claim: Length extrapolation: trained at ctx 2048, tested at 16k, xLSTM[7:1] perplexity stays 8.92 while Llama blows up to 337.83.
results.setup: 1.3B models, 300B SlimPajama tokens, trained with context length 2048, SlimPajama validation set
results.table: Figure 7 right panel, row xLSTM[7:1], column SlimPajama (300B) ppl at 16k

results.claim: On PALOMA, xLSTM[1:0] has lower perplexity than Mamba in 568 of 571 text domains.
results.metric: share of domains with lower ppl
results.setup: 1.3B models after 300B tokens; 571 PALOMA domains (16 of 18 sources)
results.note: The sentence is split by a page break; the 568/571 is vs Mamba, 486/571 (85.1%) vs Llama, 570/571 (99.8%) vs RWKV-4.
results.quote: xLSTM[1:0] has in 568 out of 571 (99.5%) text domains a lower perplexity

results.claim: PALOMA average perplexity at 1.3B: xLSTM[1:0] 11.58, Llama 12.04, Mamba 11.84, RWKV-4 13.18.
results.table: Table 4, 1.3B block, row xLSTM[1:0], column Average

results.claim: Scaling: xLSTM is better than Mamba by a margin similar to Mamba over Llama, with all models sharing similar scaling slope.
results.setup: 125M, 350M, 760M, 1.3B at 300B tokens; extrapolation to larger models is the authors' inference from four points
results.quote: The scaling behavior indicates that for larger models xLSTM will continue to perform favourable compared to Transformers and State-Space models.

results.claim: Inference: xLSTM scales linearly in generation time; Llama is quadratic and goes OOM at small batch sizes, so xLSTM reaches the highest throughput at 1.3B on an A100-80GB.
results.setup: 1.3B models, batch size 1 and pre-fill 16 for generation time; HuggingFace implementations of Mamba, Llama (static KV cache), RWKV; torch.compile did not work for full Transformer cache or Mamba
results.note: Throughput and time values are in a figure only, not in the text.
results.quote: Figure 9 shows the linear scaling of the xLSTM and the other recurrent models Mamba and RWKV-4 compared to the quadratic scaling of Llama.

results.claim: Exponential gating with memory mixing lets xLSTM solve state-tracking formal language tasks that Transformers and SSMs cannot (e.g. parity).
results.setup: Formal-language suite after Deletang et al 2023; 2-block models; train length up to 40, eval lengths 40 to 256; scaled accuracy; 3 LRs x 2 seeds
results.quote: Models such as Transformers or State Space Models without memory mixing (no state tracking) cannot solve, e.g. regular grammars like the parity task.

results.claim: Long Range Arena: xLSTM has the best mean rank (1.6) of six models, but Mamba has the best average accuracy of the five tasks.
results.setup: Five LRA tasks (Retrieval, ListOps, G-Image, RGB-Image, Pathfinder); S5/LRU hyperparameters plus LR search; xLSTM = better of xLSTM[1:0]/[0:1] on validation
results.note: Table 6 average accuracies: Mamba 0.765, RWKV-4 0.757, xLSTM 0.761 (column order as in text dump).

results.claim: Compute: all models trained over three months on 128 nodes of 8 A100 GPUs; more than 95% went to language modeling experiments.
results.quote: We developed and trained all our models and baselines over the course of three months on a cluster with 128 nodes of eight NVIDIA A100 GPUs each.

results.claim: Authors concede mLSTM CUDA kernels are about 4 times slower than FlashAttention or the Mamba scan.
results.setup: Current implementation at time of writing
results.note: The 'about 4 times slower' phrase breaks across a line in the text.
results.quote: Faster CUDA kernels could be obtained in the vein of FlashAttention.

limits: Authors: sLSTM memory mixing prevents parallelization; its CUDA kernel is under two times slower than mLSTM, which is itself about 4 times slower than FlashAttention or Mamba's scan.
Authors: forget gate initialization must be chosen carefully; matrix memory is fixed-size so it might overload at contexts beyond 16k.
Authors: architecture and hyperparameters not fully optimized, especially at larger sizes; extensive optimization needed to reach full potential.

Largest model is 1.3B and 300B tokens; claims about larger models rest on extrapolating four-point scaling curves. A 2.7B 15B-token xLSTM[7:1] run underperforms (attributed to slower early convergence).
Baselines: RWKV-5/6 and HGRN2 only at 15B tokens; 300B comparison uses only RWKV-4, Llama, Mamba. RWKV-4 re-implemented; learning rates for Llama and Mamba taken from Gu and Dao.
No seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests for LM perplexity or downstream results; some margins are small (e.g. 58.48 vs 58.41 average at 1.3B).
Inference speed results are only in Fig 9 and compare HuggingFace baseline implementations where torch.compile failed for Mamba and the full Transformer cache.
Text inconsistencies: Table 3/4 captions say 250M while sizes are 350M; text says 'maximal throughput in Figure 9 (left)' while it is the right panel.
